body.text: The student protests of 2026 have altered the political conversation in India, and few in the Congress party have watched the shift as closely as Jairam Ramesh. As the party’s communications-in-charge and general secretary, a four-time Rajya Sabha member and a former Union Minister, Ramesh has spent the past two years trying to convert public disenchantment with Prime Minister Narendra Modi into organisational strength on the ground.

In this conversation with Amit Baruah for Speak Easy, Ramesh spoke about the changed register of Rahul Gandhi’s public communication, the party’s troubled relationship with television news, and what he described as a deliberate effort to prune genuine voters from India’s electoral rolls under the Special Intensive Revision process (SIR). He also addressed, without evasion, the Congress’s own record on representation in Karnataka.
Edited excerpts

The mood in the country has definitely changed after the student protests. What led up to those protests, and what does it mean for India now, politically? Tell us about this changed mood. How is it going to work for the Congress?

There’s certainly a lot more disillusionment with the Prime Minister and his brand of politics—both the substance and the style. It’s up to us now to convert that disillusionment. There had been growing disappointment and disenchantment, but now I think it’s complete disillusionment. And it’s up to the party to convert that into electoral support. I think clearly the Prime Minister’s narrative has run its course, and people are tired of the sloganeering, the name-calling, the defaming, and his desperate attempts—clutching at straws virtually—to communicate to the student generation.
Like he went to Shri Ram College?

Yeah, going on to social media, going to colleges, interacting with students—the narrative is not selling. The substance is not selling, the style is not selling, because I think he’s got it completely wrong. And I think people are simply tired of the divisiveness in politics, tired of the perennial name-calling, the perennial defamation, the perennial running down of anything that happened before 2014. There is this theology that India is India only after 2014. So whether this translates into electoral support—four elections are coming up very shortly, early next year, and then Gujarat later in 2027, not very far off from the Lok Sabha election in 2029—remains to be seen.

But elections have their own dynamic. We have to fight not only the BJP, but we’re also fighting the Election Commission of India, which is carrying out mass deletions—instead of adding voters, which is the normal process—in the name of updating electoral rolls. This is nothing short of disenfranchisement, particularly of those sections of society who would be inclined to support the Congress party. So we have challenges. I know that there is disillusionment, which is why we have to strengthen our organisation and the outreach that our leadership — particularly Mr Rahul Gandhi — has undertaken in relation to the student community. But it is wrong to think that this outreach started after June of 2026. What is the Bharat Jodo Yatra all about? Mr Gandhi walking 140 days, 4,000 kilometres, Kanyakumari to Kashmir, and the Bharat Jodo Nyay Yatra from Manipur to Bombay over a two-and-a-half-month period, 6,000 kilometres. That was mass contact.

But it seems the way Rahul Gandhi addresses the press has changed. His last press conference—he’s using a lot of slides, pictures. He’s standing, he’s no longer sitting. I’m saying, when you’re sitting and talking versus this—there’s a change. And obviously he has an acceptability among younger people. He doesn’t have to try.

It’s certainly punchier, certainly far more focused. It’s a new style—going out onto a stage, making a presentation, three or four slides with very powerful, take-home messages, conveyed in very simple language. For example, long before the BJP protests and the student protests at Jantar Mantar, on the 17th of May, in Kota, at the first of the “Chhatron Ki Goonj” (Echo of Students) programmes, he had one slide, a telling slide, which said that families spend more on coaching centres than the government of India spends on public investment in education. That’s something that hits you. It’s a very compelling statistic. He’s done this in Kota, Dehradun, Prayagraj, Pune, and now Indore, and he’s probably going to have about 28 to 30 of these interactions. But these are interactions in the true sense of the term.
Even his press conferences are different from before.

Yeah, he gets young men, young women, and he likes stories. His method of communication is story-anchored. He tells stories and he allows others to tell stories. It’s dialogic. It’s not monologic. He’s getting people from the audience, young boys, young girls, to tell their stories. The PM’s approach to communication is very top-down—“I know everything, and I’m going to tell you what is to be done.” He’s the Sarvagyani (theomniscient one). That’s not communication. That’s a demagogic dialogue.
Considering Instagram was a key medium in the protests, would you say your party is also focusing more on Instagram to reach young people?

Over the last couple of years, the party has pulled up and has been very aggressive on social media. Mr Gandhi has been ubiquitous and aggressive, but the party too. And it’s extraordinary—the BJP was once known as the proverbial tiger when it came to communication, and the Congress as the proverbial elephant. Today, people no longer say that.
Does that credit go to you?

No, it doesn’t. I think it’s collective, but very substantially, the credit must go to Mr Gandhi. The way he went to Great Nicobar—everybody was concerned about it, but he went there, spent a couple of days, and conveyed the message from the Nicobar area itself on the ecological devastation being caused. There are numerous such instances.
The “Chhatron Ki Goonj” interactions. The language he uses is very conversational, he uses English and Hindi. He’s not bound by convention.

That’s the new generation. There is growing disenchantment, growing disquiet. People want jobs, affordable education, and productive opportunities. They’re fed up with the politics of polarisation and the politics of defamation. It’s not a question of taking credit. The Congress recognised it was far lagging behind in the communications game, and Mr Gandhi led from the front, but it was a collective team effort.

I also want to ask about images in politics. The BJP put in a lot of work to create this so-called Pappu image of Mr Gandhi. But in the last couple of months, particularly since the 20th of July, the kind of ridicule made of Mr Modi has come as a big surprise to me.

As far as Mr Gandhi was concerned, the transformational event was the Bharat Jodo Yatra. People often asked me, is it a different Rahul Gandhi? No, I said. It’s the real Mr Gandhi who is visible in the Bharat Jodo Yatra—144 days, day in, day out, early morning 5:30 to 8 o’clock at night, walking, meeting, talking to people. It’s a superhuman endeavour; not many people have done it in Indian politics. And it conveyed a completely different image of Mr Gandhi, contrary to what the BJP’s image managers were trying to project. The transformation in Mr Gandhi’s public persona has evolved over time, but the fall in Mr Modi’s persona has been very precipitous.
You see two images—him doing these videos, and then that image of him reading from a chit in front of President Putin.

I would say, the real Mr Modi is basically all about optics, and stage management. There’s no spontaneity, It’s in his communication; the strict rules, no interactions with the press. He’s the first and only Prime Minister never to have had a structured interaction with the media in the last 12 years. And the one interaction he had, in the 2024 election, he declared himself a non-biological being. So it’s better not to have one.
You can barely call it an interaction.
Yeah, the questions are given, the answers are given, and it’s just photo ops.
How would you prepare for 2029?

The transformation in Mr Gandhi’s public persona—the Bharat Jodo Yatra was the transformational moment. Over the last four or five years, the election campaign of 2024, where he held the Constitution of India up, the Red Book, and made that the defining issue—that paid rich dividends to the Congress party and its allies. Mr Modi, who had asked for “400 paar,” ended up getting 240 seats. He’s a minority Prime Minister; he wouldn’t have become Prime Minister without the support of the TDP and the JD(U). The fall in Mr Modi’s credibility, even within his own ecosystem—people who otherwise may have voted for him, or given him the benefit of the doubt, are no longer prepared to. It’s been very sudden. His whole response on social media exposed him brutally. Rises are often meteoric, but falls are equally sharp, and that’s what has happened in the case of Mr Modi.

When Rahul Gandhi uses the slogan “smash the patriarchy,” and even his calls for social justice, it looks to me sometimes that he’s talking about a transformational politics well above electoral politics.

He’s been saying this for at least a decade. Even during the Bharat Jodo Yatra, this became the three pillars of the yatra: the fight for social justice, the fight against economic inequality, and the fight against political authoritarianism. That’s what he kept saying everywhere—that we are undertaking this yatra for social justice, against polarisation, and against political dictatorship. Those were the three pillars, and it continued. The successor to the Bharat Jodo Yatra, deliberately, was the Bharat Jodo Nyay Yatra, which is when the idea of the five nyays—“mahila nyay, yuva nyay, kisan nyay, samajik nyay, and shramik nyay” (Justice for women, justice for youth, justice for farmers, Social justice, and justice for workers)—formed the plan for the 2024 election. After all, the first line of the Preamble to our Constitution is justice. The French Revolution gave us liberty, equality, fraternity, but the Preamble to the Indian Constitution places justice before liberty, equality, and fraternity. That’s the sequence: justice, liberty, equality, fraternity. And it specifies justice as social, economic, and political. A very deliberate choice by the founding fathers.

How does this fit with your Karnataka government, for instance—no woman in the council of ministers? And second, there have been instances of Bengali-speaking Muslims being harassed by the Bengaluru police.

I don’t think you should take specific instances and generalise. It’s a legitimate question—I’m not running shy of it. Should there be greater representation for women in political life, in organisational posts, in ministerial positions? Of course, who can argue against it? We are the party that gave India its only woman Prime Minister, and what a Prime Minister she was—still recalled and remembered. But I don’t want to take specific instances and generalise from that.

There are certain gaps. Should there be more women in the Karnataka cabinet? Of course, undoubtedly. I’m sure Mr Gandhi is of the same view. But in politics, so many considerations come into play, and trade-offs have to be made—trade-offs that may appear far from the ideal we espouse. I take that criticism, but it doesn’t dilute the commitment to social justice or to giving representation to different sections of society. After all, it was both Mr Gandhi as Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and Mr Kharge as LOP in the Rajya Sabha who wrote to the Prime Minister on the 20th of August on the caste census—on the way it has been deliberately weakened, the way the questions are framed, particularly question 10 in the list of 40 questions in the population enumeration. You can always pick one example and say, but what about this. Sure, there are a lot of examples, and I’m not running away from it.

Moving to the electoral challenges ahead—in Uttar Pradesh, for instance, a big state, you’ve got eight or nine Lok Sabha seats. But your organisational base there is very weak. Some people think you did well because of Akhilesh Yadav.

I think it was a symbiotic relationship. During the Bharat Jodo Nyay Yatra, at the field level, at the worker level, there was convergence between the Congress and the Samajwadi Party. The narrative got amplified by the Samajwadi Party workers and leaders. The alliance clicked in UP, and because it clicked, the BJP juggernaut was halted. The 240 seats that Mr Modi was able to manage was largely because the BJP was halted in UP, and it was halted because of the alliance. No question about it.
How do you transform this mood into an electoral defeat for the BJP—in UP, in Punjab, elsewhere?

In Punjab, we are fighting on our own. In UP, obviously, we are in an alliance; the seat-sharing discussions are going on. There are issues specific to each state—in UP, the Ram temple donation issue, which is a national issue but it is anchored in what has happened in Ayodhya and so on. One of the things that has happened in the last two-and-a-half years, after our AICC session at Belagavi in December 2024 to commemorate the hundredth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi becoming Congress president—the only year he was Congress president—we launched the “Sangathan Srijan Abhiyan” (campaign to rejuvenate the organisation), radically changing the way the District Congress Committee (DCC) presidents, the cutting edge of the organisation, are appointed and the functions they’re entrusted with. We have about 700 of them appointed through a new process of broader consultation. No elections to these posts, but with broader consultation, more younger people are involved; the average age is around 45 to 50, and there’s broader representation across social groups. Another 200 to 250 will be appointed. That’s one major transformation.

The second focus has been the appointment of Booth-Level Agents (BLAs), because with the SIR process, you need booth-level presence—not just during elections but in the run-up, in the process of updating electoral rolls. We have been weak at the cutting edge—at the district level, the mandal level, the block and booth level. Organisationally we have been weak, and that has reflected in electoral outcomes. But in the last two years there’s been a determined effort by Mr Gandhi, Mr Kharge, and others to remedy this: the DCC presence, and the sharper, more ruthless focus on the appointment of BLAs.

On the SIR—I’ve grown up in a country where the Election Commission’s messaging was that people must come out and vote, must register, must make sure their names are on the rolls, and that the Commission is there to help. Today the reverse seems to be happening. What’s the sense as a political party?

It’s clear the whole purpose of an updation exercise should be to bring new people into the electoral process. Here, the objective seems to be to eliminate people from it. It’s happened in Bihar, in Assam—and in Assam it was combined with gerrymandering, redrawing the electoral map.
And strangely, the entire National Register of Citizens (NRC) process there is frozen. Nothing has moved on that.

This was in support of the BJP’s electoral polarisation agenda. It happened also in Jammu and Kashmir. That’s one of the reasons we were dead opposed to the Delimitation Bill, brought in on the 16th and 17th of April, which didn’t get the two-thirds majority. The Home Minister is still trying to get his two-thirds majority—he split the Trinamool Congress, he split the Shiv Sena, he hasn’t yet prorogued the Lok Sabha; it’s been 24 days since it was adjourned sine die.

But going back to your question, the SIR seems clearly intended to prune the electoral rolls. 15 per cent of the electoral roll — and this isn’t my statistic, it’s from the former Chief Election Commissioner himself—have gone out of the rolls through the SIR process. That’s much beyond what mortality and migration statistics would account for. And there’s no question that only Indian citizens should be voting. But when genuine, legitimate citizens—retired foreign service officers, retired IAS officers, former judges, even the family of Nandalal Bose, who illustrated the original Constitution of India in 1949-50—find themselves completely disenfranchised, there is a much deeper, diabolical motive at work. The confidence in the Election Commission of India, a constitutional body, has been completely shattered. It’s done nothing to restore that confidence.
The kind of autonomy that Mr Lyngdoh, Mr Seshan, and others gave the Commission was quite unprecedented, and was cited even abroad as a success story.
Or the great Sukumar Sen, who managed the elections of 1952 and 1957— He was one. There were no three election commissioners. One of the real architects of our electoral democracy.

There’s a system of appointments that has been completely undermined—whether it’s the CBI or the Election Commission, though the Commission differs from the CBI in its powers and constitutional authority. What can be done to make sure these bodies function in a way that benefits the citizen and electoral democracy, irrespective of who is in power?

We changed the system for appointing the CBI director. We have a committee now, but it’s weighed heavily in favour of the executive, and the executive decides who to appoint. Only pro forma consultations take place with the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha when it comes to the appointment of the director of the CBI.
And we saw how one CBI director was removed.

When the top—in this case the Prime Minister and Home Minister—decide that these constitutional or statutory bodies should be subservient, that’s what happens. But even a statutory body is governed by a law passed by Parliament. Dr Manmohan Singh used to say autonomy is a state of mind—people should realise and exercise their autonomy. There’s no reason the Election Commission of India should be subservient to the executive, because the Constitution gives it adequate powers. I created a statutory body, the National Green Tribunal, in 2010. It functioned independently; now it’s reduced to a rubber-stamping body. There’s no reason, because the powers exist. You have to discover the strength. Mr Seshan didn’t invent new powers for himself. He took the existing powers and enforced them to clean up the system.

He said in a famous interview to Frontline that previous election commissioners used to sit in the room of the law minister’s PA, and even took permission from the law minister to buy a copy of the Constitution. It may be overstating the case, but he made a point.

Mr Seshan was the master of hyperbole. I worked with him, he was a family friend. I was very fond of him. But as Chief Election Commissioner, what he did was take the law passed by Parliament and say, I’m going to implement this. He didn’t ask for any additional powers.
And even those who came after him—Mr Lyngdoh, a classic example, O.P. Rawat, Mr Qureshi.
There are a lot of people who have stood up and said, no, these are the powers, and we are not going to allow the executive to dictate to us.
Do you hope that when there is a change of government, parties like yours are thinking about restoring that independence?

Now, take the Supreme Court. There are judges speaking out through dissenting judgments, through speeches. I don’t want to take names, but in recent months I’ve seen quite a number of Supreme Court judges expressing unhappiness at government decisions and at the way the system is functioning. People in authority must realise they are protected. They are protected by law of parliament, by the Constitution, as in the case of in the case of the CEC or the CAG, which is also a constitutional body. But this institutional capture that has taken place in the new India, post-2014, capturing the judiciary, the constitutional bodies, the universities, and the less said about the media, the better.

I want to ask about that. As communications-in-charge, what is your access like?

It’s changing. The climate is changing. In the last two months, channels that blackballed us, that wouldn’t run news about us—I don’t want to take names. But channels that had completely ignored us—the recent controversy over the GDP figures was aired on which channel? I don’t want to name it, but everybody knows that channel’s relationship with the establishment.
And newspapers?

It’s a fact. There are pockets of independence. You can still get the news. But there is a noticeable, discernible change in the attitude of the electronic media towards the Congress party. It started during the Bharat Jodo Yatra, but in the last three months it has accelerated. And I think the change wouldn’t have happened had the orders not come from the owners. I think the owners are now hedging their bets. This is a political market—you have to hedge bets in markets.
Well, on that note, Jairam Ramesh, thank you so much for talking to us. As you said, one thing is the mood, and the other is transforming it into results.

The mood is certainly for change. But the challenge is on us now. The people are ready for change, the youth is ready, the students are ready, the parents of students are ready. It’s up to us to harness that desire for change. And I think we will.
Amit Baruah is an independent journalist.
